Physics Is Not Impressed

Elon Musk can talk an engineer into moving a mountain. He cannot talk the rocket equation into moving. What he wants, what he believes, and the exact places where the universe sends the bill.

By Josh Pilcher
Scroll

The one opponent that does not negotiate

Physics is not impressed.

He can talk an engineer into moving a mountain. The mountain was never the obstacle. Keep scrolling.

Photograph via Steve Jurvetson, CC BY 2.0. A Starship stack leaves the pad. Everything in this report is about the difference between the power in this picture and the arithmetic that governs where it can go.

Verdict

Start with the man, because the man is the strategy. Elon Musk does not run a portfolio of companies. He runs two projects with a supply chain attached. Project one: make human life multiplanetary before something ends it here. Project two: end the fossil fuel economy before it ends the climate that project one is fleeing. SpaceX, Tesla, the satellites, the robots, the AI company folded into the rocket company in February 2026: every piece is an organ of one of those two projects.

The money is not the point, and the record proves it in the only way money can be proven: he keeps spending it on the projects. In 2008 he put his entire after-tax PayPal fortune, about $180 million, into companies that were weeks from death. He sold his houses, more than $100 million worth, and moved into a roughly $50,000 house at the rocket factory town, Starbase, that he rents from SpaceX. His 2025 Tesla pay package pays out on milestones that are the projects themselves: 20 million vehicles, a million robots, a million robotaxis. A man optimizing for wealth does not structure his life this way. A man optimizing for a second planet does.

He believes the destinations. That is the finding, and it is not close. What he does not believe, or does not need to believe, is his own calendar. The destinations have not moved in twenty-four years. The deadlines have moved constantly, and they move in a pattern: announced at maximum confidence, usually near a moment when confidence is worth money, then quietly reissued after the date passes. Delivered hardware at his companies arrives about twice as late as promised. Mars dates arrive a full launch window late, every time, and there has never been an exception.

So the honest question is not whether he is serious. He is. The question is what actually stands between the serious man and the destinations. His legend says the obstacle is physics, the one opponent his reality distortion field cannot charm. The record says something more precise and less flattering to everyone, including his critics. Physics does not forbid Mars. Physics prices Mars, and the price is quoted in a currency he has not yet minted: tanker flights by the dozen, reliability proven across hundreds of flights, a megawatt of power running for a year on another planet. On the ground, the legend mostly collapses. The affordable car was not killed by physics. It was killed by cost. The robotaxi is not waiting on physics. It is waiting on proof, the statistical kind, which cannot be hurried by confidence. Only the robot, Optimus, is truly fighting physics, and there the arithmetic is the harshest in this report: the machine carries about three hours of hard work in its chest.

Texas is where he chose to fight all of this, and Texas just changed the terms. He moved the empire to the state that would let him build. On November 3, the voters of that state replaced the government he built the relationship with. Physics is not the only force in his life that does not negotiate. It is just the only one that never will.

Chapter One

What He Actually Wants

It cannot be the money. He keeps spending the money on the same two projects he wrote down in 2006.

Begin in 2006, because he wrote it down. On August 2, 2006, Tesla published a document called The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan, and its stated purpose was plain: “to help expedite the move from a mine-and-burn hydrocarbon economy towards a solar electric economy.” The plan was four lines long. Build a sports car. Use that money to build an affordable car. Use that money to build an even more affordable car. While doing the above, also provide zero emission electric power generation options. Then: “Don’t tell anyone.”

Twenty years later the document reads less like a joke and more like a contract he has been executing ever since. The sports car happened. The affordable cars happened, at higher prices than promised, which is a later chapter. The power generation happened through SolarCity, folded into Tesla in 2016. The sequels kept the same shape. The 2016 plan restated the destination as sustainable energy and added solar roofs, batteries, and self-driving. The 2023 plan, the first one not signed by Musk personally, put numbers on the end state: 240 terawatt-hours of storage, 30 terawatts of renewable generation, a $10 trillion build-out, and the claim of zero insurmountable resource challenges. The destination sentence never changed. Only the map grew.

SpaceX is the older company and the deeper project. It was incorporated in March 2002, out of a 2001 idea called Mars Oasis: land a small greenhouse on Mars, grow plants in Martian soil, and use the photograph to restart public interest in space. The greenhouse never flew. The company it produced has flown more mass to orbit than the rest of the world combined. Its stated mission is to revolutionize space technology with the ultimate goal of making life multiplanetary. Note the structure. The mission is not rockets. Rockets are the method. The mission is a second address for the species.

Once you see the two projects, the corporate sprawl stops looking like sprawl. Starlink, the satellite network, is the cash engine of the Mars project. In SpaceX’s 2025 financial year, filed in its May 2026 prospectus, Starlink, which SpaceX files as its Connectivity segment, produced $11.4 billion of the company’s $18.7 billion in revenue, and its $4.4 billion of operating income made it the only profitable segment in the building. Starship, the Mars vehicle, consumed about $3.0 billion of research spending in the same year, and more than $15 billion cumulatively. The loop is closed and deliberate: the network sells internet from orbit, the profit builds the ship, and the ship is required to launch the network’s next generation of satellites. The business funds the mission that the business needs. That is not a conglomerate. That is a supply chain pointed at Mars.

Tesla’s 2025 shows the second project at a harder moment. Revenue was $94.8 billion, down 3 percent, the first decline in the company’s history. Deliveries were 1.64 million vehicles, down 8.6 percent. Net income was $3.8 billion. The car business is no longer the growth story it was, and Musk’s own attention has moved to the parts of Tesla that serve the longer arc: the robotaxi network and the robot. In September 2025, Tesla’s fourth master plan rewrote the mission sentence again, this time toward “sustainable abundance,” with AI and robotics at the center. Read through the two-project lens, the pivot is legible: if the energy transition stalls at the level of cars people choose to buy, robots and autonomy are the lever that does not ask permission.

The rest of the empire slots into the same frame. In February 2026, SpaceX acquired xAI, Musk’s AI company, valuing the combination at about $1.25 trillion: the intelligence layer sits inside the rocket company now, where the satellites and the compute are. Neuralink, with 21 implant patients as of January 2026, works on the interface between the brain and that intelligence. The Boring Company digs. None of these is a wealth vehicle in any normal sense. Each one is a component: transport off Earth, energy on Earth, intelligence to run both, and a way for human minds to keep up with the intelligence.

And the wealth itself behaves like fuel, not like a destination. The 2008 allocation is the clearest evidence ever offered: roughly $100 million to SpaceX, $70 million to Tesla, $10 million to SolarCity, out of about $180 million, all of it, into companies with a real chance of taking it to zero. He takes no cash salary. The homes went. The current pay package, approved by Tesla shareholders in November 2025, could be worth up to $1 trillion on paper, and it pays nothing unless the projects hit numbers like 20 million vehicles delivered in total, a million working robots, and an $8.5 trillion Tesla. Even the compensation is denominated in the mission.

So: what does Elon actually want? He wants a city on Mars and an Earth that runs on sunlight, and he has organized the largest private fortune in history as the working capital for those two builds. Everything else in this report is about the distance between that sentence and reality, measured in the only units that do not care about him.

Chapter Two

The Destination Is Real. The Dates Are a Tool.

The destination has not moved in twenty-four years. The calendar has never once held. Both facts are the strategy.

The strongest evidence that he believes the destinations is that he has paid for the belief when paying hurt. Belief that costs nothing is branding. Belief that nearly bankrupts you, twice, is data.

December 2008 is the exhibit. SpaceX’s first three Falcon 1 rockets had failed. The fourth reached orbit on September 28, 2008, and it had to: there was no money for a fifth. Tesla, at the same moment, held roughly $9 million in cash and was weeks from being unable to make payroll. The rescue financing closed in the final days of December, anchored by Musk himself; Tesla’s own S-1 filing records $40 million of convertible notes issued across that winter, with the largest single related-party line being Musk’s trust at about $20.4 million. Three days before Christmas, on December 23, NASA awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract to resupply the space station. Two companies were saved inside one week, and both saves ran through the same man’s balance sheet and nerve. The popular version of that week has the Tesla deal closing on Christmas Eve in the last hour it legally could. That detail comes from Musk’s own telling years later. The filings record the months, not the hour. Hold both facts: the legend is embroidered, and the underlying bet was real.

Now set that against the deadline ledger, which is the longest consistent dataset in his career.

Full self-driving was “complete autonomy in approximately two years” in December 2015. It is November 2026. Tesla’s system remains a supervised, Level 2 driver assist product, renamed FSD (Supervised) in 2024, and the company conceded in January 2025 that cars built with its third-generation hardware will need upgrades to do what was promised for them. A million robotaxis were promised by the end of 2020, at Autonomy Day in April 2019. The actual count at the end of 2020 was zero. The first paid rides came in June 2025, in Austin, in company cars, with a safety monitor in the passenger seat. Unsupervised rides began in January 2026, on a subset of the fleet.

Starship was going to reach orbit “in about six months” in September 2019. Its first orbital flight was September 28, 2026. Mars cargo missions were announced for 2022, with crew in 2024, at his 2017 architecture speech. Neither window was flown. In September 2024 he promised five uncrewed Starships in the 2026 Mars window. In February 2026, SpaceX abandoned that window and put the Moon first. The company’s own website now offers Mars cargo no earlier than 2028.

The pattern is measurable, which is what makes it useful. Count how long delivered hardware actually took against the first firm date: the Optimus prototype arrived essentially on time, a factor of 1.0. The Cybertruck took twice as long as promised, a factor of 2.0. The Model 3 ramp to 5,000 cars a week took about twice the promised span. Falcon Heavy, announced in 2011 for 2013, flew in February 2018, a factor of 3.4. Starship’s first orbit took 14 times the promised span. Across the delivered set, the average slip is a little over two, unless you include Starship’s orbit, which drags it to four and a half. The rule for reading any Musk date is therefore not cynicism. It is arithmetic: multiply by two for hardware, and for anything involving Mars, add at least one full window, because every Mars date he has ever given has missed by at least one.

Why give dates you will miss? Because in his system, the date is not a forecast. It is an instrument, and it does three jobs. It recruits: engineers join the company whose deadline feels like destiny. It finances: on April 22, 2019, Autonomy Day promised a million robotaxis and a Tesla worth $500 billion on autonomy alone; within two weeks Tesla had launched and upsized a capital raise of more than $2 billion, with the autonomy story doing the selling. And it disciplines his own organizations, which run on the pressure of impossible public commitments the way other firms run on quarterly targets. A judge, dismissing an investor suit over the autonomy claims in 2024, called the statements corporate puffery. As a defense it worked. As a description of the method, it is close to complete.

The market, for its part, prices the destination and ignores the calendar. Tesla trades at about $380 a share, a market value near $1.5 trillion, at more than 400 times trailing earnings, while Toyota trades at roughly nine times. Investors are not buying car profits at that multiple. They are buying the same two projects, at a probability they set for themselves. Musk’s gift is that he made the destinations feel inevitable enough to fund at that price. His tell is that he spends the credibility on dates, which are renewable, rather than on destinations, which are not.

Verdict on belief: he believes the stories. He does not believe the timelines, and neither should you. Treat every destination as sincere and every date as a bid.

Chapter Three

The Pace, In Numbers

Falcon’s pace is an operating fact proven across hundreds of flights. Starship’s pace is fourteen flights and an orbit six weeks old.

Strip away the dates entirely and ask the only question that cannot be spun: what is actually flying, and how often?

The Falcon family is the most productive launch system in history, and the numbers are not close. SpaceX flew 61 Falcon launches in 2022, then 96 in 2023, then 134 in 2024, then 165 in 2025. In 2025 the company accounted for 165 of the world’s 325 orbital launch attempts and lofted 2,213 metric tons to orbit, more than 80 percent of all the mass humanity put into space that year. Its own prospectus, a document with legal liability attached, claims the conservative version: more than 80 percent of the world’s mass to orbit, every year since 2023. One Falcon booster, B1067, flew its 37th mission in August 2026, two short of the all-time record held by the space shuttle Discovery. As of October 2, Falcon 9 alone stood at 692 launches with a 99.57 percent success rate, and the Falcon family passed 715 flights by November 7. This is what motivation, money, and twenty years of iteration actually bought: a solved problem, flown every two days.

Notice, though, the shape of the curve. Growth is decelerating: 57 percent, then 40 percent, then 23 percent. And 2026 is planned as a plateau, not a record. Through early November the company had flown 122 Falcon launches, an annualized pace of about 144, which lands exactly on the guidance its president gave publicly: 140 to 145 Falcon launches for the year, a deliberate taper as the company shifts its weight to Starship. Anyone who extends the 2022 to 2025 curve and predicts 200 launches in 2026 is extrapolating a growth rate that has already halved twice, into a year that was guided down on purpose.

Starship is the other dataset, and it must be read whole. Fourteen full-stack flights since April 2023. The first thirteen were suborbital by design. Flight 14, on September 28, 2026, was the first to reach orbit, deploying 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites. Boosters have been caught by the launch tower three times, in October 2024 and twice more by March 2025, and not since. A booster has been reflown once. And here is the list that governs everything after this chapter: no ship has ever been caught. No ship has ever been reflown. No ship has ever transferred propellant to another ship in orbit. The only transfer ever flown moved about five tons between tanks inside a single vehicle, in 2024. The two-ship demonstration is now expected in early 2027.

Caught, not landed

The booster comes home.

Three tower catches so far, all boosters, none since March 2025. The ship has never been caught. That asymmetry is the program in one picture.

Photograph via Steve Jurvetson, CC BY 2.0. A Super Heavy booster returns to the tower that launched it. Reuse is proven for the bottom half of the stack. The top half is the open question.

Flight 15, scheduled no earlier than November 13, attempts the two catches at once: the first V3 booster catch and the first ship catch ever tried, with 26 more Starlink satellites aboard. Musk put the odds of a first-try ship catch at 50 to 60 percent. Watch it with the right frame. It is a genuinely historic test. It is also, in the Mars ledger, step one of about five.

Now do the arithmetic the hype skips. A Mars-bound Starship, in SpaceX’s published Mars architecture, leaves Earth orbit carrying roughly 1,200 tons of propellant. It cannot lift that propellant itself; tankers must bring it up, load by load, while it waits. For a single departing ship, the tanker count is six to eight flights by Musk’s current account, sixteen by the Government Accountability Office’s estimate, and up to twenty-two by NASA’s safety advisory panel, counting the whole campaign for one lander. Those counts were all published for a lunar campaign; a filled ship is a filled ship, so they are the honest range for a Mars departure too. Take Musk’s own wave plan from May 2025: five uncrewed ships in the first wave. At his tanker count, that wave needs 35 to 45 Starship launches inside a few weeks, because cryogenic fuel boils away and cannot be banked across a year. At the government’s count, it needs 85 to 115. The actual base from which that wave would launch: fourteen Starship flights, ever, three of them in 2026, under a Starbase license capped at 25 launches a year.

The conclusion is not that SpaceX is slow. By the standards of every organization that has ever flown rockets, SpaceX is blindingly fast. The conclusion is that “pace” is two different numbers wearing one name. Falcon’s pace is an operating fact, proven across more than 700 flights. Starship’s pace, the only pace Mars depends on, is fourteen flights and a first orbit six weeks old. The distance between those two numbers is where all the bad forecasts live.

Chapter Four

The Price List

Delta-v, engine chemistry, a 26-month calendar, and air too thin to land in. The price list, in plain language.

Here is the physics, at the level of a good high school class, because the physics itself is not complicated. What is complicated is what it multiplies.

A rocket is the only vehicle that must carry its road with it. A car burns gasoline but does not carry the highway. A rocket carries every kilogram it will ever push on, including the fuel it needs to push the fuel it will need later. That recursion is written down in one equation, published by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903, and it runs every space program on Earth.

The equation says: the velocity change you can buy, called delta-v, equals your engine’s efficiency multiplied by the logarithm of how much of your rocket is fuel. Two of those words need unpacking, and then the whole Mars argument falls out of them.

Delta-v is a budget of speed. Every leg of a trip has a price. Getting from Earth’s surface to orbit costs about 9.4 kilometers per second of it. Leaving orbit for Mars costs about 3.6 more. Getting off the surface of Mars and back into orbit there costs about 4.1. From Mars orbit, the burn back toward Earth costs another 2.1 to 2.7, and it has to be bought with fuel that was either carried the whole way or made on Mars. You do not pay these prices in money. You pay them in propellant, and the equation is the exchange rate.

Engine efficiency is called specific impulse, measured in seconds. It answers the question: for how long can one kilogram of propellant produce one kilogram of thrust? Higher is better, and chemistry sets the ceiling. The best chemical engine ever flown on a crewed program, the space shuttle’s RS-25 burning hydrogen and oxygen, achieves 452 seconds. The theoretical performance of that chemistry is about 455 seconds. The RS-25 already sits on the ceiling. No nozzle, no budget, and no pep talk moves that number, because it is set by the energy stored in chemical bonds. Starship’s Raptor engine burns methane and oxygen and sits deliberately below the ceiling, in the 365 to 380 second class in vacuum, because methane can be made on Mars, stores densely, and does not soot the engines that must be reused. It is a sensible trade. It is still a trade downward from the best chemistry allows.

Now the tyranny, in one worked example. Take the methane engine at an efficiency of 370 seconds. To buy the 9.4 kilometers per second that orbit alone costs, the equation demands that your rocket’s full mass be about 13 times its empty mass. In plain terms: 92.5 percent of what leaves the pad is propellant, before a single kilogram is allowed for tanks, engines, heat shield, or crew. Each additional kilometer per second does not add a fixed amount of fuel. It multiplies the whole stack by another third. This is why rockets are mostly fuel tank with a vehicle attached, why every kilogram of extra structure is taxed so brutally, and why the entire Starship architecture is a set of tricks for paying the equation in installments: staging, reuse, and refueling in orbit, which resets the ratio mid-journey at the cost of flying the journey many times.

Physics sets the calendar too. Earth and Mars line up for an efficient transfer once every 779.94 days, about 26 months. The crossing takes roughly eight and a half months on the cheap trajectory. Miss your window by a week and the price of the slip is not a week. It is two years. Every Mars deadline in the previous chapter should be read against that number: a slipped Mars plan does not slide, it jumps, in 26-month increments, which is why his Mars dates read 2018, 2022, 2024, 2026, 2028. And the windows are not even equal. Mars’s stretched orbit makes some windows cheap and others expensive, with the energy required varying by a factor of about 2.6 across a cycle of roughly sixteen years. Physics does not just set the schedule. It sets which years are cheap.

Mars itself charges twice for landing. Its air is a wisp: surface pressure of 6.1 millibars, about six-tenths of one percent of Earth’s. That is too thin to slow you down and thick enough to burn you. A ship arrives at five to seven kilometers per second, needs a heat shield to survive the friction, and then finds there is not enough air for parachutes to matter at scale. Every successful Mars lander finished its descent on rockets. The heaviest object ever landed there is the Perseverance rover, at 1,025 kilograms. Starship proposes to land vehicles in the 100-ton class, propulsively, nearly a hundred times the demonstrated mass, on a planet where the landing cannot be fully rehearsed on Earth. This is the one place in the Mars plan where physics itself, not engineering confidence, draws the line, and the line sits two orders of magnitude away from the plan.

Radiation is the measured part. The Curiosity rover’s radiation detector recorded 1.8 millisieverts per day on the cruise to Mars and 0.67 per day on the surface, in a quiet period with no major solar storm. Run the arithmetic on a standard mission profile, about 360 days in transit and 500 on the surface, and a crew absorbs roughly one sievert round trip. The flux is physics; Mars has no global magnetic field and almost no atmosphere to hide behind. What a sievert does to a thirty-year-old’s lifetime cancer risk is biology, and how much shielding mass a program accepts is engineering, taxed by the rocket equation on every kilogram. Sort those honestly and the radiation problem is real but bounded. It is not the wall.

The fuel plant is closer to one. Making methane and oxygen on Mars is nineteenth-century chemistry: carbon dioxide plus water, energy in, propellant out. Nobody doubts the reaction. What nobody has done is run it at scale, anywhere off Earth. A returning Starship, on the published architecture, needs about 1,200 tons of propellant. Producing that takes on the order of a megawatt of continuous electric power, sustained for more than a year, plus water mining, plus compressing an atmosphere that is six-tenths of one percent as thick as ours, plus storing cryogenic liquid through Martian seasons without it boiling away. The only fuel-making hardware ever operated on Mars is an experiment called MOXIE, which across two years produced 122 grams of oxygen in total, a peak rate of 12 grams per hour. NASA’s reference plan for getting just four astronauts off the surface calls for 25 tons of oxygen. Between the demonstration and the requirement sit roughly five orders of magnitude. Motivation does not close a gap measured in orders of magnitude. Hardware, landed and running, closes it, and none has landed.

Stack the whole price list and the shape of the problem changes. Mars is not forbidden. A single crewed sortie violates no law in this chapter. What the laws do is convert every other weakness into propellant: a heavier ship, a hungrier life support system, a tanker that delivers less than promised, a depot that leaks boiloff, each one multiplies through the mass ratio and lands on the pad as more launches inside the same narrow window. The binding constraint is that roughly ten systems that have never been demonstrated must all work in the same mission, in the same season: refueling between ships, months of low-loss storage, landing a hundred tons, deploying a megawatt of power, mining water, making and storing a thousand tons of fuel, taking off again, and keeping a crew alive in a closed loop for the better part of three years with no resupply ship coming. The probability of a chain is the product of its links. If each of ten links works nine times in ten, the chain works about one time in three.

There is a statistical version of the same wall, and it may be the hardest number in this report. NASA’s standard for commercial crew is a loss-of-crew risk no worse than 1 in 270 per mission. Starship carries no launch escape system, so its safety case must be built from flight history alone. To demonstrate 99.63 percent reliability with zero failures, at 95 percent confidence, takes about 808 consecutive successful flights. Falcon 9 earned its crew rating the slow way, across years of uncrewed flights and two dedicated abort tests before any astronaut climbed in. Starship currently has fourteen flights, three of them on its present configuration. The denominator is not a detail. The denominator is the program.

An independent check reached the same place from the mass side. In a 2024 peer-reviewed study, engineers at the German Aerospace Center built a bottom-up model of SpaceX’s published Mars plan, using the company’s own headline figures, and could not make the mission close: the system mass grew past the point where a return flight works, even assuming perfect recycling of consumables. That does not prove the plan is impossible. It proves the published version of it does not yet add up, and the burden of making it add up sits with the claimant. In February 2026, the claimant quietly moved the target: Mars delayed five to seven years, a city on the Moon first, Mars cargo no earlier than 2028 on the company’s own site. Physics had sent the bill, and for once the schedule paid it.

Chapter Five

The Battery Wall, and the Robot

The car was killed by cost, not physics. The robot is the opposite case, and its arithmetic is the harshest in this report.

Leave space and the physics gets smaller, slower, and in one case much crueler. The governing number is energy density: how much work is stored in a kilogram of battery, measured in watt-hours per kilogram. Think of it as the size of a lunchbox relative to the size of the lunch. A worker with a bigger lunch works longer between meals. A battery with a higher number drives farther, or works longer, at the same weight.

Here is the reference scale that explains the entire electric era. Gasoline stores about 12,000 watt-hours per kilogram chemically, and a combustion engine wastes so much of it that the usable figure is around 3,000. A good lithium-ion cell today stores 240 to 280. The motor wastes almost none of it, so the usable figure is about 225. After a century of engines and a decade of gigafactories, the usable gap between a kilogram of gasoline and a kilogram of battery is still about thirteen to one. Everything Musk builds on the ground lives inside that gap.

The gap closes slowly, because it is chemistry, not software. Battery energy density has improved at roughly 5 percent a year over the long run, and the recent rate is 3 to 5 percent. At 5 percent, doubling takes about fourteen years. There is no Moore’s law here, no doubling every two years, because each gain is a fight over atoms: cathodes that hold 140 to 200 milliamp-hours per gram in practice, an electrolyte that becomes unstable above about 4.3 volts, silicon anodes that swell by roughly 300 percent as they charge and crack themselves apart. The practical ceiling for the current chemistry is around 300 watt-hours per kilogram in safe, long-lived, mass-produced cells. To go materially past it, the chemistry itself must change, and the new chemistries, solid-state and lithium metal among them, are pilot lines and prototypes in late 2026, not car factories. The largest battery maker on Earth rates its own solid-state program at level four of nine.

Tesla’s own flagship cell shows where the frontier actually sits. The 4680 cell, announced at Battery Day in 2020 with a stack of improvements that were widely reported as a density breakthrough, has been measured in independent teardowns at 232.5 to 241 watt-hours per kilogram. That is at or below the roughly 253 to 260 of the supplier cell it was meant to replace. The famous “five times the energy” was five times the energy per cell, because the cell is about five times bigger. Form factor is not a breakthrough. It is a bigger lunchbox holding the same lunch.

Now the car, and an honest verdict: physics does not block the affordable electric car. Arithmetic does not either. A 300-mile car needs about 75 kilowatt-hours of usable battery. In a cheap lithium-iron-phosphate pack that battery weighs around 535 kilograms; in a lighter nickel pack, around 440. Heavy, but buildable, and built daily in China. What changed the economics was price, not density: the average battery pack fell to $108 per kilowatt-hour in 2025, with car packs at $99, and the iron-based chemistry at $81. The binding constraint on the $25,000 Tesla promised in 2020 was never the periodic table. It was the factory ledger: margins, utilization, and a Chinese cost structure Tesla could not match. The car that actually shipped, in October 2025, tells you which constraint won: a Model 3 Standard at $36,990 and a Model Y Standard at $39,990, made cheaper by removing equipment, shrinking the battery, deleting features. Fifteen speakers became seven. When physics is the blocker, decontenting is not the answer. When cost is the blocker, it is exactly the answer.

Optimus is the opposite case, and it is the one place in this report where the legend understates the problem. The robot is a biped because the world is built for bipeds, and the biped form is an energy disaster that no narrative escapes. Its battery, disclosed at AI Day in 2022 and unchanged in later reporting, holds 2.3 kilowatt-hours, roughly a fifth of the machine’s 57 kilograms before a single motor is counted. Its draw runs about 100 watts standing, 500 walking, 700 or more carrying a load. Divide the lunch by the appetite: an ideal 4.6 hours of walking, under three and a half hours of heavy work. An eight-hour shift requires the robot to average no more than 287 watts for eight straight hours. That is a shift of standing and shuffling, not of lifting and carrying. Swapping batteries or charging at every pause is not a feature of the product. It is the product, until chemistry moves, and chemistry moves at 3 to 5 percent a year for everyone on Earth.

The second wall inside the robot is heat. An electric motor’s torque comes from current, and its waste heat grows with the square of current: double the torque, quadruple the heating. The most punishing task in a warehouse, holding a heavy box still at arm’s length, does no useful work at all and produces maximum heat. Humanoid actuators typically sustain only 25 to 30 percent of their peak torque continuously before the windings approach their insulation limits or the magnets begin to lose strength permanently, somewhere past 100 degrees Celsius, inside sealed joints with no sweat and almost no surface to shed heat through. A human doing the same work dumps up to a kilowatt of heat through evaporating sweat over the whole skin, and refuels continuously. The robot’s designers chose the human shape. Physics charges the human shape human prices, without the human cooling system.

Against that arithmetic, set the claims. A price of $20,000 to $30,000 per robot, contingent on building millions a year. A production target of about 10,000 units in 2025 that Tesla missed, with no unit count ever disclosed. And Musk’s own words on the January 2026 earnings call: Optimus is “still in the R&D phase,” and “not in usage in our factories in a material way.” The man who oversells everything said that. Production has since begun at Fremont, with external deliveries pushed to the end of 2027 and no unit count disclosed. Of all his products, the robot is the one where belief, capital, and motivation run into a constraint that is genuinely not negotiable on any product-cycle timescale. The lunchbox is too small, the appetite is fixed by gravity and geometry, and the refills are measured in decades of chemistry.

Chapter Six

The One Fight That Is Not Physics

An honest sort: the small part physics actually blocks, and the statistical wall that actually binds.

The robotaxi is where this report parts company with its own headline, on purpose. Almost nothing decisive about self-driving is blocked by physics, and pretending otherwise flatters the story. The honest obstacles are statistics, proof, and cost per mile. Take them in order.

First, the physics that does exist, sorted fairly. Cameras and lidar are both optical sensors, and both are defeated by the same weather. Fog droplets are ten to a hundred micrometers across, right at the scale that scatters visible and near-infrared light most efficiently, so in dense fog a lidar’s useful range collapses from hundreds of meters to tens, and a camera’s view collapses with it. The one common sensor that fog cannot blind is radar, whose wavelength is about 3.9 millimeters, vastly larger than a droplet, and which also measures speed directly. Tesla removed radar from its cars in 2021. That was a cost and architecture decision. It was not dictated by physics; if anything, the physics argues the other way.

In clear weather, the information argument for cameras is genuinely strong. Roads, signs, and signals were designed for human eyes, and a camera array sees in all directions at once, which no human head does. But the slogan version, humans drive with eyes, so eyes suffice, smuggles a conclusion past its premises. A human is not two cameras. The brain behind the eyes runs a predictive model of the scene, fuses balance, hearing, and a swiveling head, and adapts across a range of light no single camera exposure can match. More importantly, humans driving with eyes killed 1.09 people per 100 million miles in the benchmark year the standard safety analysis is built on. Proving that cameras suffice proves sufficiency for human-level carnage. The commercial and legal bar is not human level. It is provably better than human, and the proof is the expensive part.

That proof burden is a number, and it is brutal. A classic RAND analysis priced it: to show with 95 percent confidence that a self-driving fleet’s fatality rate is 20 percent better than the human rate takes on the order of 11 billion miles of driving; merely pinning a fleet’s rate to within 20 percent of the human rate takes 8.8 billion. To show, with zero fatalities observed, that you are probably not worse than human takes about 275 million miles. Those miles are the real currency of autonomy, and they accumulate at fleet speed, not at keynote speed. Waymo, running sensor fusion with lidar, radar, and detailed maps, has accumulated about 271 million rider-only miles and roughly 500,000 paid driverless rides a week. It is only now reaching the weaker of RAND’s two thresholds, inside its chosen operating areas. Tesla does not publish rides per week, fleet size, or robotaxi revenue. What it discloses is miles: about 2.5 million cumulative paid miles by mid-2026, with unsupervised miles growing fast since. The gap between the two companies is not a sensor argument. It is a denominator argument, the same shape as the Starship reliability problem, wearing a different uniform.

The record fits that reading. A million robotaxis by the end of 2020 became a pilot in June 2025 with a safety monitor aboard, unsupervised rides for a subset of the fleet in January 2026, and service across a handful of metros since. FSD, the product customers buy, remains a supervised Level 2 system in November 2026, a decade after complete autonomy was two years away. California regulators adopted a judge’s finding of misleading marketing in December 2025; Tesla escaped suspension by renaming things. None of those milestones was set by the speed of light or the size of a droplet. They were set by the long tail of rare events, the cost of validating against it, and the price of cleaning, insuring, and supervising a fleet, which is an economics problem measured in dollars per mile. The Cybercab’s promised twenty cents a mile is a target from an October 2024 stage. Observed robotaxi fares work out on the order of two dollars a mile on typical trips. Targets are not measurements, and in this chapter the distance between them is the whole story.

So the robotaxi’s obstacle is not the universe. It is the burden of proof that any society reasonably demands before letting software drive, multiplied by a sensor bet that makes the proof longer in exactly the weather where failures cluster. That is fixable in principle by miles, money, and time. Which is to say: by the same slow denominators that govern the rockets. The legend says physics is the only opponent that does not care about him. The truer version is that proof does not care about him either, and proof is the opponent he actually faces on the ground.

Chapter Seven

Houston, Then Texas

Houston first, where the old space age is changing jobs. Then the state he chose, which changed governments last week.

Start where the standing rule starts, in Houston, because Houston is where the old space age is quietly changing jobs.

Johnson Space Center still owns the crown jewels of human spaceflight: Mission Control, which runs the space station around the clock and will run Orion; the astronaut corps; the program offices. In April 2026 the center directed Artemis II, the first crewed flight around the Moon since Apollo, on its nine-day loop. And the center is shrinking. Its civil service workforce fell from 3,147 in January 2025 to 2,643 in January 2026, a 16 percent cut in a year. The pattern underneath is the one this whole report describes, at institutional scale. Houston’s space establishment increasingly directs, certifies, and buys. The building and flying migrate to companies. Intuitive Machines, headquartered at the Houston Spaceport, has landed on the Moon twice, in February 2024 and March 2025, and tipped over both times, a reminder that the landing tax described in Chapter Four is collected from everyone, not just from billionaires. Axiom Space, also Houston, is building the suits and a station module while NASA’s own inspector general counts its delays in years. The center of gravity is moving from the agency to its contractors, and Houston’s leverage now runs through Congress and contracts rather than through hardware on its own pads.

The chosen ground

Starbase, Texas.

More than $3 billion invested and roughly 4,300 jobs. The license allows 25 launches a year. The vehicle has used at most a fifth of it.

Photograph: NOAA, public domain. The Starbase launch site on the Texas coast, early 2026. This is the ground the Mars program will be fought from, at whatever cadence the hardware allows.

Then Texas, the ground Musk chose. The reasons were never mysterious: land, speed, friendly law, and a state government that treated his arrival as a trophy. He moved in 2020. Tesla’s headquarters followed in 2021, SpaceX reincorporated from Delaware to Texas in February 2024 and moved its headquarters to Starbase, Tesla reincorporated that June, and the legislature obliged with business law written to his specifications. He invested accordingly: more than $3 billion at Starbase, roughly 4,300 direct jobs there, a gigafactory outside Austin, and $15.4 million of state-level political giving on top of his federal spending. By any measure it was the most successful corporate relocation of the decade, on both sides of the deal.

What that ground actually permits, though, is worth a number rather than a legend. The FAA license at Starbase allows 25 Starship launches a year. SpaceX has flown four Starship flights from there in 2024, five in 2025, and three so far in 2026: between 12 and 20 percent of its permit. The constraint at Boca Chica so far has not been the regulator. It has been the vehicle. The next fight is already scoped: in October 2026 the FAA opened a full environmental review of SpaceX’s request to study 100 launches a year, then 456 launches and 912 landings a year. Comments close November 30. Nothing is approved. A study ceiling is not a cadence, and any report that treats 456 as a plan has confused a permit application with a flight rate.

Giga Texas tells the same two-sided story. The plant is real and enormous, and its workforce fell from 22,777 in 2023 to 16,506 at the end of 2025, and the last year of that slide, from 21,191, was a 22 percent cut by itself, part automation, part a product mix that stopped growing. On November 6, Musk announced that Cybertruck production there will wind down around the middle of 2027, the truck that sold about 70,000 units against a line built for 250,000 a year, and that the floor space goes to the Cybercab. Texas manufacturing pace was always real for the product people buy. It was never evidence for the product they did not.

And then, on November 3, the ground moved. In the midterm elections, Governor Greg Abbott, the single largest recipient of Musk’s Texas giving at $5.5 million, lost to Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against his incentives and his redacted communications with the governor’s office. Ken Paxton lost the Senate race to James Talarico. Democrats took the Texas House and every statewide executive office, the party’s first statewide wins in three decades, on results called by the Associated Press with the official canvass still weeks away. Republicans held the state Senate. None of this stops a rocket, and Starbase’s approvals run through federal channels and a city SpaceX effectively governs. But the state layer of his Texas position, the grants, the tax abatements, the bespoke corporate law, the $1.7 billion incentive package around his chip fab project, was priced for a government that just left office. Incentives are leverage, and leverage reprices when the holder changes. He chose Texas because the politics were permissive. The physics was never going to negotiate, and now, on his chosen ground, neither will the politics. That is a constraint no amount of motivation repeals, and it arrived the same week as everything else in this report.

Chapter Eight

Two Rival Reads

Same facts, two forecasts. The conditions that decide between them have dates on them now.

Everything above supports two coherent readings of the same evidence. They disagree about which constraint binds first, and the disagreement is decidable.

Read One: physics permits it, on physics’ schedule. The destinations are real, the physics allows every one of them, and the failures are failures of calendar, not of concept. Chemistry improves 3 to 5 percent a year, windows open every 26 months, reliability denominators take hundreds of flights, and Musk’s slip factor of two on hardware is what paying the price list actually looks like from inside. On this read he is not wrong. He is early, permanently, because the universe’s schedule is slower than his fundraising schedule, and the gap between the two is the biography. What would prove it: the ship-to-ship refueling demonstration in 2027 transfers propellant at the hundred-ton scale and repeats; the Artemis IV refueling campaign lands near his six to eight flights rather than NASA’s high teens; a shipping car cell measures at or above 350 watt-hours per kilogram in an independent teardown before 2029.

Read Two: the wall is the chain, and the ledger. Mars does not fail on any single law of physics. It fails on compound closure: ten undemonstrated systems that must all work in the same mission and the same window, each taxed exponentially by the rocket equation, while the ground businesses fail on the things motivation was supposed to fix: a $25,000 car delivered as a $36,990 decontented one, a robot still in research and development by its inventor’s own admission, an autonomy program a decade into a two-year promise. On this read, “physics” is the alibi that converts execution misses into heroism, and the tell is that the same 3 to 5 percent chemistry constrains CATL and BYD too, yet their affordable cars exist. What would prove it: the tanker count lands in the high teens; Optimus external sales slip past 2027 or arrive at $50,000 or more; Tesla quietly restores radar or holds a fair-weather geofence while Waymo expands into weather Tesla will not enter.

The reads share the facts. They differ on the forecast, and the forecast has dates on it now. By the end of 2028, the refueling demonstration, the Artemis campaign count, and the first external Optimus deliveries will have graded both.

Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Each one settles an argument made above.

  • 1Starship Flight 15, no earlier than November 13, 2026. The first attempted catch of a returning ship, alongside a V3 booster catch, with 26 more Starlink V3 satellites aboard. Musk rates the ship catch at 50 to 60 percent on the first try. A success starts the reuse denominator that every later number depends on. A failure costs a window of testing time, not the program.
  • 2The Starbase environmental review, comments closing November 30, 2026. Whether the study of 100, then 456, launches a year survives scoping decides Starbase’s realistic ceiling for the decade. The current license, 25 a year, has never been the binding constraint. Watch whether the review treats cadence as a planning number or a physical one.
  • 3The ship-to-ship propellant transfer demonstration, expected in early 2027. The single test underneath every Moon and Mars date in this report. Tonnes transferred, boiloff measured over weeks, and a repeat performance are the three facts that matter. Another slip past 2027 moves the 2028 Mars window from unlikely to impossible.
  • 4The Artemis IV refueling campaign, 2028. Count the flights it actually takes to fill one lander. Near six to eight, his numbers were right and the panels were timid. In the high teens or beyond, the compound-closure read wins and every Mars date derived from the low count goes with it.
  • 5Optimus external deliveries, targeted for the end of 2027, and the hardware remedy for older Tesla cars. A robot that ships to outside customers, at a stated price, with a published unit count, is a product. Another year of internal pilots is a program. In parallel, whether Tesla upgrades the older cars’ computers free, at its own cost, or sends owners to a trade-in desk will say more about how to read the next decade of promises than any keynote.
